# Verification, Feedback, and Learning {#sec-feedback-verification-trust}

::: {.epigraph}
> "Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence!"
>
> — Edsger W. Dijkstra, *Notes on Structured Programming*, second edition [@Dijkstra1970Notes, p. 7]
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
**Governing question:** *How do returned signals become trustworthy, what do they mean for the architecture work, and what should improve or be retained as a result?*

**Core thesis:** *Raw tool returns must be qualified through verification before feedback can guide the next design action and accumulate into durable learning across runs.*
:::

A clean simulator exit or a zero-violation timing report is not proof of a working chip; raw tool returns become architectural evidence only when rigorously qualified against physical constraints, operating corners, and formal invariants. In an autonomous design loop, treating unvetted tool logs as ground truth invites catastrophe. An optimizer will happily exploit a missing timing constraint, an unconstrained multicycle path, or an idealized zero-delay memory model to report counterfeit performance gains.

This chapter unifies the three core disciplines that close the design loop (@fig-ch07-cover-map). *Verification* establishes the exact boundary of what an empirical simulation or formal proof mathematically demonstrates. *Feedback* translates that qualified evidence into actionable design repairs, distinguishing between infrastructure failures (license timeouts, memory exhaustion) and genuine microarchitectural flaws (deadlocks, setup violations). *Learning* accumulates those qualified observations across runs, updating surrogate models and pruning dead ends without poisoning future iterations with unvetted proxy artifacts.

The argument builds directly on machine-usable representations (@sec-data-representations-world-models), method choice (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization), and isolated execution environments (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces). Qualified feedback completes the technical engine of the autonomous loop, establishing what a single iteration proves before that evidence guides redesign or retirement; evaluating the aggregate workflow against human baselines is addressed in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect.

![**Qualifying returned signals into actionable feedback and retained learning.** Raw tool outputs pass through verification qualification to establish their validity envelope and bounded claims. Feedback routes the qualified evidence to guide revisions, further checks, or stopping decisions, while durable observations are retained for cross-run learning.](images/ch07-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch07-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which a returned signal passes through verification qualification and a bounded claim before feedback routes the next action and learning is retained."}

## Qualified Architectural Actions and Decisions {#sec-from-feedback-to-decision}

When a simulation returns cleanly or a static timing tool reports zero violations, it is tempting to treat the run as an architectural pass. Yet that return may leave an unhandled multicycle path,[^fn-mcp-c07] an unconstrained power domain, or a floating CMOS node[^fn-floating-cmos-c07] unexamined. Generating register-transfer level (RTL) candidates and establishing that they meet their requirements are different jobs. An AI-native design system must determine what its tool returns reveal about those candidates and how the results should guide redesign.

[^fn-mcp-c07]: **Multicycle paths**: A sequential path designed to require more than one clock cycle between launch and capture registers (such as complex floating-point or multi-cycle divider units). Static timing analysis tools default to enforcing single-cycle timing; an unhandled multicycle path triggers false timing violations, while an erroneous `set_multicycle_path` constraint hides true setup failures by permitting unvalidated extra clock cycles.

[^fn-floating-cmos-c07]: **Floating CMOS Node**: A condition where a CMOS gate input is not driven by any defined logic level (0 or 1), leaving its voltage uncontrolled. An intermediate input voltage can turn on both input transistors, increasing static current; noise can also produce unpredictable logic transitions.

The execution environment described in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces supplies immutable records with pinned dependencies and raw transcripts. Qualification establishes which claims those returns can support. The required check follows from the claim. Physical feasibility requires the relevant physical checks, while a claim of invariant satisfaction requires a proof over its declared model and assumptions. Empirical checks qualify observed quantities from cycle-accurate simulations, hardware emulators, or post-silicon telemetry; formal methods can establish invariant satisfaction over mathematical models under declared assumptions [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. A particular formal return must still be interpreted. A completed invocation does not guarantee that the tool proved the intended obligation.

Translating raw execution logs into architectural choices is a sequence of qualification steps, each of which can send the work back rather than forward (@fig-evidence-flow).

![**Tool returns gain architectural meaning through claim-specific result qualification.** Execution records supply returns with status and lineage; result qualification binds types, targets, and conditions; property checks test formal or physical validity; and feedback scoping defines supported claims before learning records what to revise or retain.](images/fig-evidence-flow){#fig-evidence-flow width="80%" fig-alt="Five-step flow diagram from tool return through verification and a comparison or property check to feedback and a learning step that records what to improve or retain. Side paths send incomplete returns to execution repair and invalid checks to study formulation."}

Qualifying an execution return requires separating five distinct questions:

1. Did the requested tool run execute to completion without infrastructure faults or license drops?
2. Is the returned artifact structurally and syntactically valid for downstream toolchains?
3. Is the measurement or proof valid under its declared model and assumptions, including relevant process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) conditions?
4. Which specific architectural requirement or physical constraint does the result satisfy or contradict, and which requirements remain unexamined?
5. What concrete design revision, parameter update, further check, or bounded claim does the qualified evidence support? Does it instead justify retaining the candidate or stopping work on it?

These distinctions determine what should change next. While the execution harness in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces guarantees execution integrity (isolating process exits, license drops, and memory exhaustion), verification in this chapter establishes semantic qualification (exposing false slack paths, unconstrained clocks, and vacuous formal assertions). A license timeout calls for infrastructure recovery; it provides zero evidence of candidate deficiency.

When a candidate encounters a genuine, qualified physical or timing violation, an autonomous loop should not discard the design and restart generative exploration blindly. Instead, diagnostic feedback ascends the *causal repair hierarchy*, applying interventions ordered by increasing cost and architectural disruption:

1. *Localized Physical ECO (Lowest disruption):* Gate sizing, threshold-voltage ($V_t$) swapping, buffer insertion, and pin swapping. These physical engineering change orders close near-miss negative slack paths without altering the RTL or sequential behavior.
2. *Sequential Retiming and Pipelining (Moderate disruption):* Moving flip-flops across combinational boundaries or inserting pipeline registers on latency-insensitive paths. These transformations change sequential cycle timing and require sequential equivalence checking (SEC), but preserve datapath interfaces.
3. *Structural and Algorithmic Redesign (Highest disruption):* Decomposing wide arbiters, splitting monolithic crossbars into distributed networks-on-chip, or redesigning memory hierarchies. This tier invalidates existing floorplans and requires full generative re-exploration.

Only when lower-tier interventions fail to close slack does the feedback engine escalate to higher-tier architectural mutations. Lifting a multi-cycle waveform or critical-path report into an architectural repair requires intermediate diagnostic synthesis rather than dumping raw logs into an optimizer or prompt. Conversely, a result that supports the intended claim may justify retaining the candidate for the next evaluation without changing its design. Feedback selects among these actions; whether a finding should also change the search method is a separate learning decision.

Which of these questions dominates depends on where the system sits among the three layers of @fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration. A Layer 1 point draft whose testbench came from the same model may reproduce the same omissions; a Layer 2 optimizer operating within a frozen container scoring a floorplan on proxy wirelength can game the proxy without ever violating it. A Layer 3 AI-native design system must coordinate checks across the boundaries its search can change, choosing formal, power-intent, structural, or mutation checks to cover the declared claims and expose shared blind spots.

Tool execution failures also affect how returns are qualified. An interrupted run may still supply completed measurements or proofs, provided their lineage, completion status, and scope can be established independently of the interrupted work. Outputs whose status remains uncertain are retained without treating them as completed evidence; no partial return supports the uncompleted obligation. If a timing check omits a required PVT corner, it cannot establish timing feasibility at that corner. Likewise, a missing Unified Power Format (UPF)[^fn-upf-c07] isolation check leaves the corresponding power-state behavior unqualified; a completed check that finds an isolation violation supplies evidence of a design or power-intent defect. Missing checks and demonstrated violations require different responses even when both prevent a broader feasibility claim.

[^fn-upf-c07]: **Unified Power Format (UPF)**: The standard declarative specification language for low-power design intent, defining power domains, supply nets, power-switch networks, isolation cells, and level shifters. Modern toolchains decouple logical RTL from physical power intent; RTL simulation cannot verify power-gating sequences or domain transitions without companion UPF constraints and power-state tables.

## Evaluation Signal Sources and Signoff Attrition {#sec-signal-sources-attrition}

The signals that qualification works on span a wide range of latency, spatial granularity, and physical fidelity. Analytical roofline estimators can evaluate simple kernels quickly, while cycle-accurate simulation and full-chip physical signoff may take hours. Hardware emulation provides another tradeoff, supporting long instruction traces at a higher execution rate than software simulation. For an illustrative scheduling comparison, suppose a roofline estimate takes under a millisecond and a physical signoff run takes 12–48\ hours; these are assumed latencies, not measurements or universal tool runtimes. Static timing, dynamic IR-drop,[^fn-ir-drop-c07] and design rule checking in electronic design automation (EDA) engines return different kinds of failures. An IR-drop report from RedHawk-SC may locate a violation on the die, while Cadence Tempus may identify a failing timing path. Those reports help diagnosis but do not by themselves establish which upstream architectural choice should change. Lineage binding the metric to candidate parameters, RTL revisions, tool flags, and constraints makes that investigation possible.

[^fn-ir-drop-c07]: **Dynamic IR-Drop**: Time-varying switching activity changes current demand on the power-delivery network. The resulting supply-voltage variation can reduce timing margin or threaten stored state. Analysis needs the network and activity models; an ordinary logic simulation does not measure those voltage effects.

Control theory warns that feedback delay and noise constrain how aggressively a controller can respond [@AstromMurray2008FeedbackSystems]. Architectural search is not necessarily a continuous controller, so that warning alone does not establish its stability or latency budget. It does expose the risk of proposing many changes before their physical consequences return. One arrangement uses fast, qualified proxies to steer exploration while slower signoff results recalibrate those proxies and reopen affected candidates. The system must retain which revision each delayed result checked.

Automated verification is a structural need rather than a convenience. A design with $|S|$ Boolean state bits has at most $2^{|S|}$ possible states; the subset reachable under its reset and input assumptions can be smaller. The longitudinal Wilson Research Group surveys discussed in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales place verification effort alongside persistent first-pass silicon failures, the *verification scissors*.[^fn-verification-scissors-c07] Random stimulus can leave corner-case deadlocks and races unexercised, so adding vectors alone does not establish their absence. Generative proposal velocity can widen this gap unless stage-matched qualification filters the candidate pool. In semiconductor engineering, evaluation budgets are strictly bounded by available compute and commercial tool license pools. A naive unguided generator that dumps thousands of raw proposals directly into physical synthesis and signoff timing would quickly exhaust corporate license servers and incur prohibitive costs.

Multi-fidelity screening organizes verification across progressive tiers of physical fidelity, execution latency, and license expenditure (@fig-synthesis-verification-funnel). Early millisecond-scale linting, interface compliance, and assertion checks eliminate non-viable candidates before invoking expensive, licensed static timing analysis and physical verification. The pipeline decouples two distinct recovery pathways: early syntactic, protocol, and functional rejections route directly back to the generative agent for prompt revision or abstract syntax tree (AST) repair, whereas late physical implementation closure relies on localized engineering change order (ECO) iterations (such as buffer insertion, gate sizing, and pin swapping) to repair near-miss physical timing violations without discarding the candidate and restarting the generative loop.

![**Multi-fidelity verification filters generative proposals across progressive fidelity tiers.** Schematic workflow organizing checks from millisecond-scale open-source linters through licensed static timing and physical signoff. Closed-loop recovery decouples early structural and functional repairs (routed back to generative prompt revision) from late physical timing near-misses (routed to localized engineering change orders).](images/fig-synthesis-verification-funnel){#fig-synthesis-verification-funnel width="100%" fig-alt="Flowchart of a five-tier multi-fidelity verification signoff funnel from generative candidate proposals down to tapeout-qualified GDSII or OASIS, showing feedback loops for generative repair versus localized ECO optimization."}

Rejecting a malformed proposal at parsing avoids spending resources on the later checks. Early filtering can therefore make a larger proposal stream affordable, provided the filter itself is suitable for the candidates it screens. To choose an order, consider what each check can reject, how long it takes, which artifacts it requires, and how much later work a justified rejection avoids. A cheap check belongs early when its result can support that rejection; passing it leaves the obligations addressed by later checks open. Every empirical observation entering the search loop also needs admission criteria before it is compared with anything.

## Empirical Admission Criteria {#sec-empirical-admission-criteria}

An empirical measurement needs enough context to establish what was measured before it can enter a comparison. A clean exit code may hide uninitialized cache warmup states (where cold-start misses distort instructions per cycle), uncalibrated process corners, or truncated trace intervals. The seven record elements in @tbl-measurement-record make these conditions inspectable. Together they identify the value, establish how it was extracted, and state the variation and error that limit its use.

| **Record Element** | **Question the record must answer** |
| - | - |
| Candidate identity | Which design revision, hardware configuration, software state, and workload produced the value? |
| Quantity and unit | What architectural metric was computed, how was it aggregated, and in what unit? |
| Conditions | Which tool and model versions, random-number generator seeds, and process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) conditions are relevant to this quantity? |
| Extraction status | Did the expected output artifact exist, parse under the declared schema, and retain raw logs? |
| Variation and error | What repetitions, sampling methods, numerical tolerances, or error bounds restrict the value? |
| Constraint integrity | Which versions of applicable timing constraints in Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) form, power intent (UPF), and waiver manifests were used, and how are they identified, for example by recorded SHA-256 hashes? |
| Source record | Which returned artifact, extraction procedure, and execution record support this metric, and what dependencies would be needed to reproduce it? |
: **A measurement requires identity, meaning, conditions, and limits.** These record elements establish whether a measurement is eligible for a scoped comparison; the comparison itself needs additional qualification. {#tbl-measurement-record tbl-colwidths="[28,72]"}

[^fn-constraint-auditing-c07]: **Timing constraint integrity and waiver auditing**: Automated design loops optimizing for timing slack face a subtle reward-hacking failure mode: relaxing constraints to falsely clear violations. Beyond crude `set_false_path` additions, an agent can subtly relax clock uncertainty, artificially increase maximum transition limits, alter on-chip variation derating tables, or declare optimistic multicycle path exceptions. Constraint files (SDC) must be cryptographically hashed and diff-audited against immutable baseline constraints, with all multicycle exceptions formally verified against pipeline hazard logic.

```{=latex}
\newpage
```

Passing admission criteria qualifies a metric as eligible for comparison, but does not validate the comparison itself.[^fn-constraint-auditing-c07] That judgment requires evaluating the complete experimental delta under matched operating conditions, as developed in @sec-evidence-specific-to-claim-and-scope. Before comparing candidates, however, the architect must distinguish a measured quantity from a proof that a candidate obeys a required contract. A cache's measured latency and a proof that its controller preserves transaction ordering answer different questions, even when both arrive through the same execution interface.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="A returned value must qualify before it becomes feedback"}
**Context.** Consider a hypothetical return from evaluating a prospective L2 cache configuration for the Lighthouse XR subsystem under a 3\ W thermal design power envelope. Suppose static UPF checks pass, but a bounded model checking (BMC) run encounters a setup failure, and a thermal report omits raw trace lineage. These statuses illustrate routing; the Lighthouse study has not executed.

**Application.** For the thermal value, the required context includes the activity trace, power and thermal models, applicable operating conditions, and extraction procedure. Hardware and software revisions, the instruction set architecture (ISA), compiler state, and memory timing assumptions must also be identified where they affect that activity or its interpretation. The missing raw trace lineage prevents this value from entering a comparison; unrelated completed checks retain their own scope. Passing static UPF checks neither supplies that lineage nor resolves the BMC setup failure.

**Outcome.** The setup failure routes to environment repair, and the incomplete thermal value remains unqualified. Neither return establishes a defect in the architectural candidate. Retaining that distinction prevents infrastructure failures from becoming false negative training labels.
:::

## Formal Bounds and Sequential Equivalence {#sec-formal-bounds-sequential-equivalence}

A comparative performance claim needs a matched baseline; a safety property can be checked directly against its declared model and assumptions. While dynamic simulation exercises sampled execution traces, a completed unbounded formal proof establishes that an implementation satisfies an invariant across all reachable states within those assumptions. In automated exploration loops, such proofs can establish interface protocol compliance, rule out specified control hazards, or certify equivalence before expensive downstream synthesis and place-and-route runs. A bounded search or an inconclusive run supports a narrower conclusion, so the returned proof status matters as much as the property itself.

### Proof Statuses and Contract Equivalence {#sec-proof-statuses-equivalence}

Properties (expressed as SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA)[^fn-sva-c07] for formal temporal logic proofs) specify microarchitectural contracts, while assumptions in formal tools (JasperGold, VC Formal) constrain legal input sequences, resets, and clock domains [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. When verifying simplified abstract models, counterexample-guided abstraction refinement (CEGAR) evaluates returned failure traces against the concrete RTL. *Spurious counterexamples* (artifacts of over-approximated abstraction that cannot occur in real hardware) trigger automatic model refinement, whereas *realizable counterexamples* expose genuine RTL bugs or specification errors [@ClarkeEtAl2000CEGAR].[^fn-cegar-c07]

[^fn-sva-c07]: **SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA)**: A formal property specification language extending SystemVerilog with concurrent temporal logic constructs. Unlike instantaneous software assertions, concurrent SVA expressions evaluate multi-cycle temporal sequences (e.g., verifying that a valid request is followed by an acknowledge within three cycles) across clock edges, enabling both formal model checking and simulation coverage tracking.

[^fn-cegar-c07]: **CEGAR (Counterexample-Guided Abstraction Refinement)**: A fundamental formal verification algorithm. To avoid state-space explosion, CEGAR starts by verifying a simplified (over-approximated) model of the hardware. If the solver finds a violating path, it checks whether that path is possible in the concrete model. A realizable path violates the encoded property under its assumptions; interpreting it as an RTL defect still requires the intended contract and model to agree. If the path is spurious, the abstraction is refined to exclude it and checking continues.

Beyond property checking on individual blocks, completed formal proofs can establish behavioral equivalence across representations. *Combinational equivalence checking* (CEC) compares logic between aligned state elements to check whether logic synthesis preserves gate-level truth tables. *Sequential equivalence checking* (SEC)[^fn-sec-cec-c07] checks behavioral correspondence for microarchitectural transformations that alter pipeline register boundaries, retiming stages, or transaction latencies, subject to the correspondence defined for the check [@Kropf1999FormalVerification]. At system interfaces, *assume-guarantee reasoning* modularly verifies block contracts. For example, a proof can establish that if a bus fabric satisfies transaction ordering assumptions, the connected accelerator guarantees credit-queue safety [@BenvenisteEtAl2018Contracts].

[^fn-sec-cec-c07]: **Sequential vs. Combinational Equivalence (SEC vs. CEC)**: Combinational equivalence checking (CEC) compares logic between 1-to-1 mapped flip-flops, scaling efficiently for logic synthesis signoff. Sequential equivalence checking (SEC) verifies behavioral input-output equivalence when state elements are retimed, pipelined, or restructured. Because SEC requires exploring reachability across arbitrary state-transition graphs, it faces PSPACE-complete complexity and severe state-space explosion on complex microarchitectures.

Equivalence checks define what counts as 'the same behavior,' but this definition must follow the architectural claim. CEC compares corresponding combinational functions under an agreed state correspondence. SEC additionally reasons about behavior over time; permitted retiming or latency correspondence must be part of the checking setup.

An exact-reference comparison may reject a candidate that changes interface timing, lengthens a tolerated latency, or changes ordering within what the specification permits. That mismatch can be correct for the selected reference even when the new behavior is legal. Replacing the reference with the candidate itself would evade the question rather than resolve it.

The relevant obligation is refinement. Every implementation behavior must correspond to a behavior allowed by the specification. A *refinement mapping* relates the implementation's state to the specification's state so that this correspondence can be proved [@AbadiLamport1991RefinementMappings]. The check must declare the permitted latency shifts and protocol changes in advance. A log reporting 'equivalence passed' supports only the reference and correspondence that were actually checked.

### Bounded Search and Vacuity {#sec-bounded-search-vacuity}

BMC unrolls transition relations to depth $k$ to catch shallow defects [@BiereEtAl1999BMC]. Finding no counterexample through $k$ supports a bounded claim. To establish unbounded safety, the checker must additionally establish that this depth is sufficient to cover every reachable violation, or complete a separate proof using $k$-induction or property-directed reachability (IC3/PDR) [@Bradley2011IC3; @EenEtAl2011PDR]. Increasing $k$ alone does not supply that completeness argument.

Deeper unrolling explores longer behaviors but can exhaust the solver budget (@fig-sva-bmc-coverage-depth). Shallow control structures (such as direct memory access [DMA] ring-buffer controllers) reach a complete proof at moderate depths, conditional on establishing completeness or a separate inductive proof. Complex state machines (such as multi-tile systolic array controllers) instead encounter state-space explosion and Boolean satisfiability (SAT) solver timeouts. While exact transition depths depend on the specific design and solver, BMC depth scaling alone cannot guarantee signoff closure for deep control state spaces.

![**State-space coverage diverges across control structures as bounded model checking scales.** Conceptual model showing bounded model checking unrolling transition relations to depth $k$, where shallow control logic (such as direct memory access ring-buffer controllers) reaches exhaustive formal proof through inductive completeness at moderate depths. Complex multi-tile state machines and credit-based resource arbiters hit exponential SAT solver timeouts, requiring compositional assume-guarantee contracts or inductive reachability framing.](images/fig-sva-bmc-coverage-depth){#fig-sva-bmc-coverage-depth width="80%" fig-alt="Line chart of formal state-space coverage rising with bounded model checking unroll depth across four hardware execution units alongside exponential SAT solver complexity."}

The exponential solver runtime cliff marks the boundary where bounded model checking ceases to be computationally tractable for complex multi-tile state spaces. At this cliff, search must transition from brute-force unrolling to compositional assume-guarantee contracts or inductive reachability framing.

*Safety properties* exclude forbidden behavior (such as mutual exclusion violations), while *liveness properties* require eventual progress, often under explicit fairness assumptions [@AlpernSchneider1985Liveness]. Both are trace properties, evaluated on one execution at a time, although a liveness violation may require an infinite trace. Noninterference relates executions that differ in a secret and asks whether an unprivileged observer can distinguish them. It is a *hyperproperty*,[^fn-hyper-c07] a property of a set of traces [@ClarksonSchneider2010Hyperproperties]. The paired-execution check used for this form of noninterference cannot be replaced by inspecting one execution in isolation; hyperproperties in general are not limited to pairs. SPECTECTOR checks speculative noninterference through symbolic execution under declared speculative semantics, comparing observations with and without speculation [@GuarnieriEtAl2020SPECTECTOR]. The property class therefore determines the checking problem before depth and budget are chosen.

[^fn-hyper-c07]: **Hyperproperties**: Hyperproperties describe relationships across multiple execution traces, such as constant-time execution in cryptography, where the required timing observations must not reveal differences in secrets when public inputs and relevant conditions are held fixed.

Vacuity checks ask whether an assertion succeeds without exercising the behavior it was intended to constrain [@BeerEtAl2001Vacuity].[^fn-vacuity-antecedent-c07] For example, an assertion that every accepted request eventually receives a response can pass vacuously if the environment assumptions prevent any request from being accepted. A cover query for request acceptance under the same assumptions tests whether that trigger is reachable. A witness rules out this particular source of vacuity; it does not prove the response obligation. If the cover query establishes that acceptance is unreachable, inspect the assumptions and trigger before using the assertion to support a progress claim. A bounded search without a witness leaves reachability beyond that bound unresolved.

[^fn-vacuity-antecedent-c07]: **Vacuous assertion passes**: In formal logic, a conditional implication $A \implies B$ evaluates to true whenever the antecedent $A$ is false. In hardware assertion checking, if environment assumptions or upstream wiring permanently suppress an antecedent signal (such as a request handshake never asserting), the assertion passes with a nominal 100% formal score while leaving the required consequence $B$ completely unexercised. Industrial signoff requires witness cover properties to certify that every assertion antecedent actually fired during formal verification.

Automated assertion generators (e.g., AssertLLM) require syntactic and semantic qualification, including seeded-mutant checks of whether their proposed assertions detect relevant defects [@FangEtAl2025AssertLLM; @PulavarthiEtAl2025AssertionGeneration]. Mutation testing asks a different question, assessing whether the assertion detects an introduced defect. Trigger reachability alone does not establish that sensitivity; @sec-semantic-rtl-defects develops how to assess it.

One route from bounded checking to an unbounded safety proof is $k$-induction. In the following indexing convention, the *base query* $B_k$ searches for a property violation from the initial state through step $k$. The *inductive-step query* $S_k$ searches for a transition from states $s_0$ through $s_k$ that satisfy the property to a state $s_{k+1}$ that violates it:

$$B_k = \bigvee_{j=0}^{k}\left(Init(s_0) \land \bigwedge_{i=0}^{j-1} T(s_i,s_{i+1}) \land \neg P(s_j)\right),$$

$$S_k = \bigwedge_{i=0}^{k} P(s_i) \land \bigwedge_{i=0}^{k} T(s_i,s_{i+1}) \land \neg P(s_{k+1}),$$

where $Init(s_0)$ constrains the initial state, $T(s_i, s_{i+1})$ is the hardware transition relation, and $P(s)$ is the target safety invariant. The base query considers every prefix length from zero through $k$, including traces that cannot continue; the empty transition conjunction at $j=0$ is true. If $B_k$ is unsatisfiable, no violation is reachable from $Init$ through step $k$; $Init$ must encode any reset assumptions the claim requires. If $S_k$ is unsatisfiable, every trajectory satisfying $P$ in the $k+1$ consecutive states $s_0,\ldots,s_k$ also satisfies it in the next state. Unsatisfiability of both queries establishes unbounded safety for this induction construction. A satisfiable base query instead supplies a reachable counterexample.

The inductive-step query does not require its starting state to be reachable from $Init$. A satisfying trace may therefore begin in an unreachable state, producing a *spurious inductive counterexample* rather than a hardware bug. The verifier can increase the induction depth or seek auxiliary invariants $Inv(s)$ that strengthen the property. The proof must establish the strengthened condition $P(s) \land Inv(s)$ from $Init$ and show that it is preserved by the modeled transitions. Simply assuming an auxiliary condition could exclude a real defect. PDR/IC3 takes another route, maintaining over-approximated reachability frames $F_0, F_1, \dots, F_k$ and learning clauses that block unreachable counterexamples until it finds a suitable inductive invariant or a reachable violation [@Bradley2011IC3; @EenEtAl2011PDR].

Formal verification statuses dictate distinct downstream engineering actions (@tbl-formal-result-status).

| **Formal status** | **What it establishes** | **Eligible next action** |
| - | - | - |
| **Proved** | Property holds for recorded model and assumptions under verified checking components. | Discharge the scoped architectural claim once the property and assumptions are qualified, including relevant vacuity checks. |
| **Counterexample** | A trace satisfies the violation query; its reachability and realizability depend on the query and abstraction. | Check reachability and realizability. Refine a spurious abstraction, strengthen a failed induction argument with proved invariants, or repair RTL or specification for a confirmed failure. |
| **Bounded-only** | No counterexample found through depth $k$. | Record finite bound; extend search, seek a completeness argument or separate proof, or leave unbounded safety open. |
| **Inconclusive** | Solver timed out or exceeded memory limits. | Revise abstraction, decompose assumptions, or adjust resource bounds. Never report as a pass. |
: **Formal result status dictates next technical actions in verification feedback.** Proofs discharge scoped claims; counterexamples and bounds drive targeted repairs or open records. {#tbl-formal-result-status tbl-colwidths="[20,40,40]"}

An inconclusive status establishes neither a proof nor a violation. The tool may still retain a checked bound or another partial result, which needs its own qualification. A clean process exit cannot substitute for the declared property status. Bounded-only carries a different hazard. It provides evidence only through depth $k$, and that bound must travel with the result to prevent the claim from quietly becoming an unbounded one.

## Dynamic Coverage and Mutation Testing {#sec-semantic-rtl-defects}

A proof covers what its property set, model, and assumptions name (@sec-formal-bounds-sequential-equivalence). Other claims still need suitable checks. Full system-on-chip software workloads and dynamic thermal behavior pose modeling and scale challenges for formal analysis, while cycle-accurate simulation and hardware emulation exercise long execution traces without covering every corner case. Verification suites therefore combine methods, using formal proofs for selected interface protocols, arbiters, and crossing properties, and dynamic evaluation for workload throughput, power, and end-to-end latency under the modeled conditions.

Dynamic verification pairs constrained-random simulation (Synopsys VCS, Verilator) and Universal Verification Methodology (UVM)[^fn-uvm-c07] coverage metrics [@IEEE2020UVM; @IEEE2023SystemVerilog] with hardware emulation platforms (Palladium, ZeBu, Veloce). Low-power verification combines static Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 1801 UPF power-state tables with low-power-aware simulation to verify power isolation clamping cells and level shifters across power domains [@IEEE2024UPF]. A power estimate also needs the applicable power-state transitions qualified; an RTL simulation that omits those transitions leaves their effects untested. Sampled dynamic simulation cannot prove the absence of rare corner-case bugs, as demonstrated by the historic Pentium floating-point division (FDIV) lookup table defect [@SharangpaniBarton1994FDIV; @Edelman1997PentiumDivision; @Colwell2006PentiumChronicles].

[^fn-uvm-c07]: **Universal Verification Methodology (UVM / IEEE 1800.2)**: A standardized SystemVerilog class library for building modular, transaction-level verification testbenches. UVM structures environments into reusable stimulus generators, drivers, monitors, and scoreboards, combining constrained-random stimulus generation with functional coverage metrics to test complex protocols.

::: {.callout-war-story title="The Pentium FDIV flaw and the limit of sampled testing"}
**Context:** Pre-silicon execution-unit verification passed millions of random division vectors.

**Defect:** Five omitted entries out of 1,066 in the radix-4 Sweeney-Robertson-Tocher (SRT) division programmable logic array manifested only once in 9 billion random divisions [@SharangpaniBarton1994FDIV; @Edelman1997PentiumDivision].

**Outcome:** Sampled dynamic simulation cannot guarantee defect absence in high-dimensional state spaces. A later industrial example of addressing this limitation is the use of formal verification in Intel Core i7 execution-engine validation [@KaivolaEtAl2009Corei7Formal].
:::

Sampled stimulus is one limit of dynamic coverage. The other is the checker. A testbench drafted alongside the RTL can execute defective logic without detecting the wrong outcome, especially if both inherit an omitted requirement. Syntactic validity leaves semantic and physical questions open, including clock and reset crossings, interface ordering, and power-domain isolation. The following eight examples show which checks can address those questions; they are not an empirical ranking of the defects in generated RTL.

1. **Inferred latches and combinational loops.** An incomplete assignment in intended combinational logic can imply state retention, producing a latch inference[^fn-inferred-latches-c07] or a tool diagnostic. A selected stimulus may miss the unintended behavior, and the latch introduces timing obligations such as hold checks.[^fn-hold-timing-c07] Lint and synthesis reports expose unintended storage and combinational feedback; functional tests establish only the behaviors they exercise.
2. **Clock-domain crossing (CDC) and reset-domain crossing (RDC) metastability.**[^fn-cdc-c07] An asynchronous input that changes near a receiving clock edge can leave a flip-flop metastable, with a risk that its output does not settle before downstream logic samples it. Synchronization must fit the transfer. A dual-rank synchronizer can reduce the risk for a suitable single-bit control signal, while a multi-bit transfer needs a protocol that preserves coherence, such as a properly designed asynchronous first-in, first-out buffer. Reset deassertion that violates recovery or removal timing can similarly leave state elements inconsistent. Ordinary RTL simulation does not model the analog settling process. Dedicated CDC and RDC analysis checks crossing structures, protocols, and assumptions, with formal or metastability-injection checks where appropriate.
3. **Interface handshake and memory-ordering violations.** An Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) source that waits for `READY` before asserting `VALID` can deadlock with a receiver waiting for `VALID`; dropping an unacknowledged transfer can lose data. A testbench whose receiver never stalls may miss both defects. Separately, generated logic or software that assumes sequential consistency can fail under behaviors permitted by RISC-V Weak Memory Ordering (RVWMO).[^fn-rvwmo-c07] The relevant tests must exercise those behaviors and compare them with the declared memory model; a core count alone does not determine that coverage. Interface assertions and assume-guarantee proofs can check the handshake obligations, while memory-model tests or proofs check the ordering assumptions.
4. **Bitwidth truncation and overflow.** A vector accumulator that silently drops precision can pass stimulus that never reaches the affected range. Width lint flags potential truncation; directed boundary-value tests or formal checks establish whether the implemented wraparound or saturation matches the specification.
5. **Unhandled reset states in finite state machines (FSMs).** An FSM lacking a recovery transition from an unused encoding can become stuck if a fault or unexpected control sequence places it there. FSM lint and reachability analysis help identify missing behavior; a fault-injection claim also needs a model of how the fault enters the state. Simulation detects the problem only when its stimulus and fault model exercise it.
6. **Four-state $1\text{'bx}$ optimism.** Under ordinary IEEE 1800 semantics, `if (1'bx)` takes the `else` branch [@IEEE2023SystemVerilog]. That choice can hide uncertainty about an uninitialized or otherwise unknown control value. X is a simulation value, not a particular physical voltage. The corresponding hardware may hold either logic value, or the model may be abstracting a different electrical problem.[^fn-x-optimism-c07] X-propagation-aware simulation and formal checks that account for unknown initial state can expose behaviors masked by the ordinary branch semantics. Their unknown-value assumptions remain part of the check.
7. **Missing isolation and level shifting across power domains.** Required level shifting depends on the voltage compatibility of the crossing; required isolation depends on power states and the receiving interface's needs [@IEEE2024UPF]. Omitting required isolation can feed an invalid logic level into an active domain. In a simplified CMOS inverter, an input in the range $V_{tn} < V_{in} < V_{dd} - |V_{tp}|$ can turn on both transistor networks and draw crowbar current. Static UPF checks and low-power-aware simulation address the declared structure and modeled behavior; they do not quantify all electrical consequences, including latchup risk.[^fn-latchup-c07] Those require suitable device and power-network analysis.
8. **Silent false paths and multicycle overrides in SDC constraints.** An optimizer can hide a real timing violation by inserting an unjustified `set_false_path` or `set_multicycle_path` directive. A clean report then leaves the underlying path unchecked or checked against an inappropriate requirement. Independent constraint review and SDC lint can challenge the exception; the timing report alone cannot, because the engine follows the supplied constraints. The 850\ ps instance in @sec-timing-exception-attacks illustrates a reported absence of negative slack despite a real setup failure.

[^fn-inferred-latches-c07]: **Inferred Latches**: In synchronous digital design, combinational logic must assign output values under every possible input condition. If an RTL conditional (`if-else` or `case`) omits an assignment branch, synthesis tools must insert a physical level-sensitive latch to hold state. Unlike edge-triggered flip-flops, transparent latches complicate static timing analysis with time borrowing and create severe race conditions and testability failures.

[^fn-hold-timing-c07]: **Hold Timing**: A physical timing constraint ensuring that data remains stable at a flip-flop's input for a minimum duration after the active clock edge. Unlike setup timing violations, which can be mitigated post-silicon by reducing the operating clock frequency, hold violations represent fatal physical race conditions where fast data overtakes the clock edge, permanently corrupting state regardless of frequency.

[^fn-cdc-c07]: **CDC/RDC Metastability**: A clock or reset crossing can violate a receiving element's timing requirements and create a risk of metastability or inconsistent state. Synchronization and crossing protocols reduce that risk under declared assumptions; a digital simulation without a metastability model does not measure the analog settling behavior.

[^fn-rvwmo-c07]: **RISC-V Weak Memory Ordering (RVWMO)**: The official memory consistency model of the RISC-V ISA, which permits hardware to reorder loads and stores to different addresses unless explicitly constrained by memory fence instructions (`FENCE`). Out-of-order execution pipelines and store buffers can expose subtle multi-core data races that are completely undetectable in single-core or sequentially consistent simulations.

[^fn-x-optimism-c07]: **Four-State Logic and X-Optimism**: Four-state simulation distinguishes 0, 1, Z (high impedance), and X (unknown). For the single-bit condition `if (1'bx)`, ordinary SystemVerilog semantics select the `else` branch, potentially masking uncertainty [@IEEE2023SystemVerilog]. X can represent uninitialized state, conflicting drivers, or another unknown modeled value. It does not identify a particular physical voltage or establish metastability.

[^fn-latchup-c07]: **Latchup**: A destructive condition in CMOS circuits where parasitic bipolar transistors form a low-impedance path between power and ground rails, causing excessive current flow that can permanently damage the silicon unless power is removed.

Using the same large language model (LLM) family to generate RTL and its testbench risks reproducing the same omissions, creating a *self-verification paradox*. Mutation testing challenges the verification suite by introducing synthetic faults (such as inverted branch conditions, altered arithmetic operators, or stuck-at registers) and measuring which non-equivalent mutants[^fn-equivalent-mutants-c07] the testbench detects.[^fn-red-teaming-c07] While structural coverage records which code lines or state transitions were exercised, mutation analysis directly evaluates whether the test suite observes incorrect behavior when faults occur. Published RISC-V compliance testing demonstrates that surviving mutants effectively highlight blind spots in conventional directed suites [@HerdtEtAl2021MutationCompliance].

Empirical signoff audits expose both the necessity of checker diversity and the severe limits of simulation-based coverage metrics (@fig-ch07-defect-discovery-modalities). In the OpenHW Group's tapeout-grade CV32E40P RISC-V core verification signoff audit ($N=47$ resolved RTL defects), non-simulation modalities uncovered $59.6\%$ of all bugs (@fig-ch07-defect-discovery-modalities a). Formal SVA property checking and peer code inspection each accounted for $27.7\%$ of bug discoveries, exposing deep control bugs such as memory-stall deadlocks, CSR privilege violations, and exception priority inversions. In contrast, randomized constrained-random UVM simulation identified only $4.3\%$ of the defects, despite consuming weeks of compute. Concurrently, evaluating testbench efficacy against 1,240 injected microarchitectural mutation faults reveals a severe *testbench vacuity paradox* (@fig-ch07-defect-discovery-modalities b). A conventional directed test suite achieves $88.4\%$ line coverage but detects only $34.8\%$ of injected faults, leaving a 53.6-point vacuity gap. Even industry-standard constrained-random UVM achieves $98.6\%$ line coverage while allowing $41.4\%$ of functional mutation bugs to escape completely unnoticed [@HerdtEtAl2021MutationCompliance]. Only formally guided symbolic execution with SystemVerilog Assertions closes the vacuity gap entirely.

![**Formal checks and code review dominate defect discovery as line coverage masks fault escapes.** (a) In the OpenHW Group CV32E40P audit ($N=47$), non-simulation modalities uncovered $59.6\%$ of bugs (formal SVA and peer review each $27.7\%$), while constrained-random UVM caught only $4.3\%$. (b) Across 1,240 injected mutation faults [@HerdtEtAl2021MutationCompliance], directed tests achieve $88.4\%$ line coverage but detect only $34.8\%$ of mutants (a 53.6-point vacuity gap), and UVM leaves $41.4\%$ unobserved; exhaustive formal SVA achieves $100\%$ detection.](images/fig-ch07-defect-discovery-modalities.png){#fig-ch07-defect-discovery-modalities width="100%" fig-alt="Two-panel chart in which subplot (a) shows a horizontal bar chart of defect discovery across verification modalities for the OpenHW CV32E40P core, and subplot (b) compares line and branch coverage against mutation kill rates across four test methodologies to illustrate the testbench vacuity paradox."}

One proposed use of automation is mutation-directed property generation. Rather than mutating flattened post-synthesis gate netlists (where logic minimization and technology mapping destroy high-level signal semantics and create synthetic nets), mutations are injected at the source RTL abstract syntax tree (AST) level (such as modifying conditional branches, operator polarities, or state transitions). Non-equivalent mutants are identified within a bounded formal equivalence budget, and the simulation suite runs against them. For a surviving mutant, the environment returns the mutation details and source context to a model that proposes an SVA property or a directed testbench sequence. The suite must then run again to establish whether the new check detects the fault while accepting the correct design. Killing the retained mutants supports a claim about detection of that tested fault set. It does not establish that all corner cases have been found, that the original specification is complete, or that the generator and checker have no shared omissions.

An evaluator drawn from the generator's own model family may repeat the same omissions. Such a second opinion can corroborate an answer without independently challenging it, the distinction developed in @fig-independent-checks and treated as a red-team target in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect. A design environment therefore needs fault-detection measurements alongside structural coverage, and claim-specific checks whose assumptions remain visible. Formal proof engines supply one such check for declared properties; their proofs still depend on the specification they are given.

## Scoping a Comparison to the Claim It Supports {#sec-evidence-specific-to-claim-and-scope}

A correctness proof or a qualified functional testbench does not by itself rank two candidates by performance. Once individual measurements meet the admission criteria, an empirical claim that one design outperforms a baseline still needs an evaluation that separates the hardware effect from confounding variation under matched workloads. That comparison requires control over compiler lowering, memory initial states, simulator versions, and operating corners. An isolated delta cannot distinguish a hardware gain from simulation jitter, cold-start cache artifacts, or compiler phase-ordering shifts without those controls.

Every comparison binds candidate and comparator revisions to a measured difference and uncertainty model under explicit operating conditions (@fig-claim-frame).

![**Comparative claim frames bind candidate and baseline designs to measured deltas.** Compared designs (candidate and comparator) map to measured results (quantities, units, differences, and uncertainty). These remain conditional on experimental scope (workloads, architectural state, tool versions, PVT corners, and check nonclaims). A change in evaluation scope creates a distinct comparison rather than an interchangeable measurement.](images/fig-claim-frame){#fig-claim-frame width="80%" fig-alt="Three-column diagram of a comparison frame. Candidate and comparator feed a measured quantity, difference, and uncertainty. These are bounded by workload and design state, tool conditions, and check scope."}

For a matched set of architectural evaluation cases $c_j \in \mathcal{C}$ (representing identical benchmark inputs, initial cache states, and PVT operating corners), the paired difference is:

$$
d_j = y(\text{candidate}, c_j) - y(\text{comparator}, c_j),
$$

where $y(\cdot)$ denotes the evaluated architectural metric. For positive per-benchmark performance ratios, a geometric mean preserves comparisons when the normalization reference changes, provided the benchmark set and weights remain fixed [@FlemingWallace1986HowNotToLie]. If the claim concerns total execution time for a specified workload mix, aggregate execution times using that mix before forming a ratio.

Confounding factors (simulator versions, compiler flags, thermal states, and cache warmup intervals) can create apparent performance deltas independent of architectural interventions [@GutierrezEtAl2014SourcesOfError; @PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity]. For paired observations with temporal dependence, block resampling[^fn-block-bootstrap-c07] estimates uncertainty while preserving local dependence within sampled blocks [@Kunsch1989BlockBootstrap]. The block choice and sampling assumptions remain part of the interval's qualification. A comparison also needs a decision margin $m$, the smallest difference in $y$ that would change the architectural decision, declared before measurement. An interval crossing zero leaves the direction unresolved. An interval wholly inside $\pm m$ supports the narrower conclusion that the difference is below the declared practical margin, even if its direction is unresolved. This difference-below-decision-margin status is retained under @tbl-feedback-destinations without forcing a design update.

[^fn-block-bootstrap-c07]: **Block Bootstrapping**: A non-parametric resampling technique designed for time-series data with temporal dependence. In computer systems, performance metrics like instructions per cycle and memory latency cluster into execution phases. Standard independent and identically distributed ($i.i.d.$) resampling destroys this temporal structure and severely underestimates variance; block bootstrapping resamples contiguous chunks of execution traces to preserve local autocorrelation.

A decision-relevant improvement needs evidence relative to $m$ in the metric's favorable direction. With candidate-minus-comparator differences, an interval wholly below $-m$ supports such an improvement for a lower-is-better metric such as latency; an interval wholly above $m$ does so for a higher-is-better metric such as throughput. An interval that excludes zero but crosses the favorable decision threshold supports a direction without resolving whether the gain is large enough to change the decision. Further measurement is justified when resolving that uncertainty could change the choice; otherwise, the comparison can be retained with its limit explicit.

Selecting the top performer among thousands of noisy evaluations adds a second hazard, the selection bias that @sec-support-limits introduced as the optimizer's curse.[^fn-winners-curse-c07] The estimates used to select a winner tend to overstate its advantage. The apparent margin therefore needs an independent confirmatory measurement before it supports an improvement claim.

[^fn-winners-curse-c07]: **Winner's Curse**: Selection among noisy estimates can overstate the selected candidate's value. Independent confirmation addresses that selected result; multiple-comparison procedures address related inference problems under their own assumptions and do not repair systematic model error.

::: {.callout-law title="The Winner's Curse in Candidate Optimization Sweeps"}
**The Classical Principle:** Selection among noisy estimates can favor optimistic error. The winner's curse names this hazard in competitive bidding [@CapenEtAl1971CompetitiveBidding; @Thaler1988WinnersCurse]; the optimizer's curse applies the selection argument more generally. For a fixed finite candidate set, let $v_i$ be candidate $i$'s true value, with larger values preferred, and let $\hat v_i$ be an unbiased estimate. Selecting $I=\arg\max_i\hat v_i$ gives $\mathbb{E}[\hat v_I-v_I]\geq0$, with expectation over repeated evaluations [@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse]. The inequality is strict if noise can cause selection of a candidate whose true value is below the optimum. This is an average selection effect, not a guarantee that every winning estimate is too high or has the largest measurement error.

**The Hardware Trap:** A sweep can select a microarchitecture partly because a sampled workload phase or random tool variation favored it. A deterministic simulator omission presents a distinct hazard because repeated runs with the same model can reproduce the same misleading advantage.

**The Architectural Antidote:** Confirm the selected design on fresh seeds where randomness matters and on held-out workload phases. Challenge suspected model omissions with a check that can observe them; reseeding the same simulator is insufficient (@sec-law-winners-curse in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).
:::

## Qualifying Proxies and Calibration {#sec-proxy-mismatch-metric-gaming-and-calibration}

Independent confirmatory evaluation tests a selected candidate, but exploration also needs faster ways to decide which candidates to test. Analytical cost models, cycle-approximate simulators, and learned surrogates serve that role. When a surrogate diverges from physical behavior, search can exploit modeling omissions such as ignored dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) bank serialization, interconnect contention, or thermal dissipation limits. This is microarchitectural proxy gaming (@sec-architecture-20-ontology) [@Goodhart1975MonetaryManagement; @Strathern1997Goodhart]. A better surrogate score then need not yield a better implementable design. Qualifying the proxy requires separating *observed qualification strata*, regions represented by paired proxy and reference measurements, from *unsampled evaluation gaps* (@fig-trust-calibration) [@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS; @SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint; @ForresterSobesterKeane2008Surrogate].

![**Discrete qualification strata expose unsampled proxy evaluation gaps.** Paired proxy and reference observations anchor confidence only at discrete sampled strata (Q1, Q2, Q3). Unsampled gaps between strata, and regions beyond sampled support, risk severe divergence between surrogate predictions and reference evaluations [@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS; @SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint; @ForresterSobesterKeane2008Surrogate]. Curves represent conceptual search progression, not measured data.](images/fig-trust-calibration){#fig-trust-calibration width="80%" fig-alt="Conceptual line chart with three separate green qualification strata in the left-hand range. Paired proxy and stronger-reference markers appear in each stratum, while a dashed white band marks an unsampled gap between the first two. The curves diverge as search continues into an unqualified right-hand range. No plotted curve is measured data."}

When search enters an unsampled gap, the existing observations may no longer justify the surrogate's reported error bounds, even if those bounds remain narrow. Matched reference measurements in the new region test whether rankings remain useful. Without that qualification, a candidate that looks attractive to the proxy may fail physical closure; a confident score does not settle the question.

The verification loop must therefore audit the proxy itself. Evaluating its fitness for use pairs specific failure modes with diagnostic checks (@tbl-proxy-diagnostics). Comparisons across performance, power, and area also need an explicit decision rule. Pareto dominance identifies when one candidate is at least as good in every objective and better in at least one; a scalar objective instead encodes particular preferences or tradeoffs, which must be declared [@Deb2001MultiObjective].

| **Concern** | **Diagnostic check** | **What an adverse result means** |
| - | - | - |
| **Proxy mismatch** | Compare proxy with stronger reference measurement on matched cases against the tolerance required for the intended use. | Disagreement beyond that tolerance leaves the intended use unsupported; other uses require separate checks. |
| **Observed coverage** | Map candidate and tool dimensions; identify unsampled gaps. | Evidence does not qualify candidates outside sampled strata. |
| **Held-out agreement** | Measure error and ranking stability against decision margins on held-out cases. | Excessive error limits quantitative estimates; unstable rankings limit ordering for the declared use, even within observed strata. |
| **Confounding** | Hold versions and budgets fixed using matched contrasts. | Measured difference does not identify proposed architectural cause. |
| **Variability** | Repeat stochastic flows and report dispersion. | If uncertainty prevents resolving the declared decision margin, the point estimate alone cannot justify the decision. |
| **Selection bias** | Re-evaluate selected candidate on fresh, unseen cases. | Original apparent margin is not independently confirmed. |
: **Each weakness requires a distinct diagnostic.** Adverse results eliminate specific inferences without making other diagnoses interchangeable. {#tbl-proxy-diagnostics tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

The third column limits what the architect can infer from each diagnostic. Failure on one task need not make the surrogate useless for every other task, but another use still needs its own qualification. A proxy unreliable for fine ranking might support coarse screening only if its false-acceptance and false-rejection behavior is acceptable for that screen. Passing the observed checks also does not establish behavior outside their qualified scope.

**Case study: scalar compression and masked write traffic.** The hazard of evaluating candidates through a reduced scalar proxy is demonstrated when a scoring metric compresses multi-dimensional behavior into a single figure of merit. In an empirical study evaluating systolic array aspect ratios under SCALE-Sim [@RajEtAl2025ScaleSimV3], both the $32 \times 32$ baseline and a candidate $16 \times 64$ array achieved an identical cycle count (13,917 cycles) and identical average compute utilization (41.2%), producing an exact tie under the declared scalar objective ($S = \text{total cycles}/\bar{U}_{\text{frac}} = 33,782.40$).

However, examining secondary physical metrics omitted by the scalar proxy exposes a severe trade-off (@fig-proxy-mismatch). The $16 \times 64$ candidate reported 409,726 modeled DRAM-word writes compared to 204,863 for the $32 \times 32$ baseline, representing a 100% explosion in off-chip memory traffic. The baseline strictly dominates the candidate across these two physical dimensions: equal latency with half the memory traffic. A scalar evaluator blind to memory traffic treats the designs as equivalent, risking selecting an implementation that induces severe bus contention or thermal throttling at the system level.

::: {.callout-law title="The Whac-a-Mole Regression Effect"}
**The Caution:** Optimizing a single scalar metric can hide trade-offs in quantities the score omits. Those quantities need their own checks; improvement in one metric does not establish their acceptability or imply that they must regress.

**The Hardware Trap:** Reading a tied score as interchangeable behavior hides the write-count difference. That omission becomes consequential if a later decision depends on the memory system, even though this run does not determine the physical consequence.

**The Architectural Antidote:** Freeze every decision quantity that the scoped claim needs before execution, and keep modeled returns distinct from physical measurements. A future memory study must test contention, timing, and energy under its own bound configuration rather than reading those consequences out of the retained SCALE-Sim write counts (@sec-law-whac-a-mole in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-proxy-mismatch
#| fig-cap: |
#|   **Modeled traffic exposes model-local dominance masked by the scalar score.** Across retained SCALE-Sim total cycles (horizontal axis, lower is better) and modeled DRAM-word writes (vertical axis, lower is better), the 32 by 32 baseline and shared 16 by 64 candidate tie at 13,917 cycles while reporting 204,863 and 409,726 modeled writes, respectively. The baseline therefore dominates the candidate only across these two retained SCALE-Sim quantities. This post-run observation does not alter the frozen study outcome or establish physical traffic, contention, timing, or energy [@RajEtAl2025ScaleSimV3].
#| out-width: "100%"
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of evaluated systolic array shapes across retained SCALE-Sim total cycles and modeled DRAM-word writes, showing the 32 by 32 baseline and 16 by 64 candidate tied at 13,917 cycles while reporting 204,863 and 409,726 modeled writes, respectively."

import json
from pathlib import Path
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import _python.plots as _ap
from _python.plots import COLORS, apply_style

apply_style()

_root = Path(_ap.__file__).resolve().parents[2]
result_path = _root / "data/studies/ai_systolic_array_study/recorded/reference/study_results.json"
if not result_path.exists():
    result_path = _root / "labs/examples/ai_systolic_array_study/recorded/reference/study_results.json"
result = json.loads(result_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
arm_runs = [r for r in result["evaluations"] if r["arm"] in {"model", "conventional"}]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 3.5))
fig.subplots_adjust(left=0.18, right=0.95, top=0.95, bottom=0.15)

ax.set_xlabel("SCALE-Sim total cycles (lower is better)", fontsize=6.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Modeled DRAM-word writes (lower is better)", fontsize=6.5)

seen = set()
for r in arm_runs:
    key = (r["workload_id"], r["array_rows"], r["array_cols"])
    if key in seen:
        continue
    seen.add(key)

    cid = r["candidate_id"]
    cycles = r["metrics"]["total_cycles"]
    dram_writes = r["metrics"]["dram_writes"]
    label = cid.replace("model_baseline_", "").replace("ai_wide_", "").replace("ai_extreme_", "").replace("ai_compact_", "").replace("conventional_baseline_", "").replace("heuristic_", "")

    if "32x32" in label:
        ax.plot(cycles, dram_writes, marker="o", markersize=5, color=COLORS["blue"])
        ax.text(cycles + 300, dram_writes - 12000, f"Baseline {label}", color=COLORS["ink"], fontsize=5.5, ha="left", va="top")
    elif "16x64" in label:
        ax.plot(cycles, dram_writes, marker="X", markersize=5, color=COLORS["red"])
        ax.text(cycles + 300, dram_writes + 15000, f"Shared candidate\n{label}", color=COLORS["ink"], fontsize=5.5, ha="left", va="bottom")
    else:
        ax.plot(cycles, dram_writes, marker="s", markersize=4, color=COLORS["orange"], alpha=0.6)
        ax.text(cycles + 300, dram_writes, label, color=COLORS["ink"], fontsize=5, ha="left", va="center", alpha=0.7)

baseline_cycles = next(
    r["metrics"]["total_cycles"]
    for r in arm_runs
    if r["workload_id"] == "original"
    and r["array_rows"] == 32
    and r["array_cols"] == 32
)
ax.axvline(x=baseline_cycles, color=COLORS["grid"], linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8, zorder=0)
ax.set_xlim(12800, 27800)

ax.tick_params(axis="both", labelsize=5.9, length=2.5, width=0.6, pad=2)
ax.grid(True, color=COLORS["grid"], linewidth=0.55, zorder=0)
for spine in ["top", "right"]:
    ax.spines[spine].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["left"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])
ax.spines["bottom"].set_color(COLORS["ink"])

plt.show()
```

## Outcome, Mechanism, and Counterfactual Reasoning {#sec-outcome-mechanism-counterfactual}

A proxy qualified for a particular use in @sec-proxy-mismatch-metric-gaming-and-calibration does not by itself explain why a candidate performs better. An observed top-line *outcome* and its proposed explanatory *mechanism* require separate judgments (@tbl-outcome-mechanism). When an automated optimizer modifies a microarchitectural feature, recording an improvement in top-line latency or throughput does not prove that the intended mechanism produced the gain. For instance, a cache resizing candidate might post improved frame rendering times not because larger static random-access memory (SRAM) capacity reduced conflict misses, but because incidental compiler instruction alignment masked a memory bus serialization stall. Establishing architectural causality requires counterfactual testing through controlled contrast experiments that hold confounding compiler, memory, and operating variables fixed while probing the isolated mechanism.

| **Evaluation question** | **Possible qualified status** | **Why the distinction matters** |
| - | - | - |
| **Did requested quantity change in declared direction?** | Supported, contradicted, or unresolved. | Latency confidence interval spanning zero leaves improvement unresolved. |
| **Did proposed intermediate effect occur?** | Supported, contradicted, unresolved, or untested. | Qualified reduction in capacity misses confirms bounded cache effect. |
| **Did intermediate effect cause the outcome?** | Supported only by distinguishing contrast under identification assumptions. | Lower miss count alone does not prove it caused tail-latency reduction. |
| **What did the check fundamentally not observe?** | Explicit nonclaims. | Cache-local results do not establish thermal stability or functional correctness. |
: **Outcome and mechanism remain separate results.** Intermediate effects cannot substitute for unresolved architectural comparisons. {#tbl-outcome-mechanism tbl-colwidths="[34,30,36]"}

Generated explanations need the same scrutiny. A fluent causal narrative about a candidate's success is a hypothesis until measurements test it. Useful observations include performance-counter deltas, cycle-accurate stall breakdowns, queue-occupancy profiles, and ablation traces in which the mechanism is switched off and the outcome remeasured.

To distinguish the two explanations above, compare the original and enlarged cache at each of two controlled instruction alignments, using the same workload and holding the remaining compiler, memory, and operating settings fixed. If changing alignment reproduces the gain while adding capacity at fixed alignment yields no resolved benefit, the contrast would challenge the capacity explanation. A gain from added capacity at both alignments would support a capacity contribution. Both factors may contribute: an alignment benefit does not by itself rule out a capacity benefit. Miss counts and bus-stall breakdowns would then help test the proposed path from capacity through fewer misses to lower latency. If the capacity effect depends on alignment, retain that interaction in the explanation rather than attributing the gain to capacity alone. These contrasts support causal interpretation only insofar as the intervention changes the intended factor and the relevant conditions remain matched.

The prospective Lighthouse L2 cache configuration shows what the test has to separate. A larger L2 might reduce off-chip DRAM traffic enough to improve 99th-percentile frame latency. Evaluating that benefit also requires counting added SRAM area, leakage, tag-array lookup delay, and network-on-chip (NoC) queue pressure. The same capacity increase that raises the hit rate can lengthen the tag lookup or serialize NoC packets and make tail latency worse. Queue-occupancy profiles and latency distributions would help distinguish the capacity benefit from that failure; a hit-rate delta alone cannot.

These are trade-off hypotheses rather than measured results. The telemetry also needs checks for simulator artifacts, including a fixed-latency queueing model, omitted DRAM refresh cycles, or an unconstrained register-file assumption in the compiler backend. Each can produce an apparent mechanism that exists only in the model. A mechanism supported by the distinguishing contrast and those model checks remains qualified by the identification assumptions and the model's scope. Otherwise, it remains contradicted, unresolved, or untested according to the evidence in @tbl-outcome-mechanism; a supported outcome can still be retained separately.

## Verification and Falsification Boundaries {#sec-independent-checks-and-correlated-errors}

Qualifying individual results leaves a further question: do those results cover the requirements of the design? Assurance engineering structures this argument by linking high-level performance and correctness claims to supporting checks and explicit assumptions [@Kelly2004GSN]. For each requirement, identify the relevant checks, the conditions under which their results apply, and any remaining gap.

A successful check supports only the obligations it addresses. A check that could falsify a claim is useful even when passing it cannot establish the claim in full. Across physical limits, functional contracts, and quality-of-service bounds, the task is to determine how the checks fit together and where further evidence is needed. The following subsections develop that argument through requirement mapping, check fidelity, and shared blind spots.
### Mapping Requirements to Verification Toolchains {#sec-mapping-requirements-toolchains}

A complex compute subsystem needs checks matched to each physical requirement. Static timing engines such as Cadence Tempus check setup and hold timing across specified modes and corners [@Cadence2021Tempus]. Power-integrity analysis such as RedHawk-SC addresses voltage drop and electromigration limits,[^fn-em-c07] while physical verification such as Calibre checks layout against the applicable rule deck. The limiting conditions differ by property; a corner that stresses setup timing need not be the limiting corner for hold timing or leakage, and dynamic IR-drop also depends on switching activity. The verification plan must therefore name the relevant PVT conditions, activity assumptions, extraction models, and rules for each check. A pass covers those declared conditions; a nominal point estimate or a functional testbench does not establish physical feasibility across them.

[^fn-em-c07]: **Electromigration (EM)**: The gradual displacement of metal atoms in a conductor caused by high current densities over time. This atomic movement leads to wire thinning and eventual open circuits, degrading chip reliability.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="Architectural requirements remain unresolved for distinct structural reasons"}
**Context.** The prospective Lighthouse compute subsystem requirements span physical constraints, performance service-level agreements, and correctness invariants.

**Application.** Physical limits require suitable analysis under explicit corners; performance claims need matched workload measurements with quantified uncertainty. A formal proof can discharge a named correctness invariant under its model and assumptions, while other functional requirements may need simulation, tests, or additional properties. RedHawk-SC can supply power-integrity analysis; a thermal-analysis path must be separately selected and bound before making a thermal claim.

**Outcome.** A requirement remains open if its returned check is unqualified or no check has been assigned to it. For an unqualified return, investigate the qualification gap and repair or rerun the check as needed. Where no check exists, assign a suitable evaluation path. This mapping states what the prospective subsystem would need; it does not report completed Lighthouse verification.
:::

### Scoping Observations and Check Fidelity {#sec-check-fidelity-scoping}

Every tool check in an architecture flow operates within the observational horizon @sec-data-representations-world-models records for its source, and qualification is where that horizon becomes a limit on the claim. A syntax linter verifies port lists and grammar without ensuring that logic will synthesize cleanly; a cycle-level simulator measures instruction throughput across modeled queues while remaining blind to physical layout congestion, clock-tree skew, or parasitic wire $RC$ delays.[^fn-rc-delay-c07] Upstream proxy speedups or downstream physical passes cannot expand a tool's semantic coverage beyond what its underlying mathematical model observes.

[^fn-rc-delay-c07]: **Parasitic RC Delays**: In physical layout, microscopic metal wires have inherent electrical resistance (R) and capacitance (C). Resistance and capacitance set the scale of interconnect delay, while the wire geometry, driver, load, and distributed network determine the path delay. Wire delay can limit timing even when individual logic gates become faster.

Static timing analysis makes that horizon concrete. For a simplified edge-triggered, single-clock example with a combinational timing graph, let $G=(V, E)$ contain timing pins as vertices and propagation arcs as edges. The static timing analysis (STA) engine propagates arrival times through this graph under the supplied constraints and corner models. Let $T_{\text{arr, max}}$ measure the worst-case data arrival relative to the launch-clock edge (incorporating maximum clock-to-Q delay, data-path delay, and path-specific on-chip variation derating factors), let positive $t_{\text{skew}}$ mean that the capture clock arrives later than the launch clock, and let $t_{\text{uncertainty}}$ account for clock phase jitter and pessimism margins. The setup condition for the latest arrival is:

$$
T_{\text{arr, max}} \le T_{\text{req}} = T_{\text{clk}} - t_{\text{setup}} + t_{\text{skew}} - t_{\text{uncertainty}}
$$

For the hold check, $T_{\text{arr, min}}$ instead denotes the earliest arrival (incorporating minimum clock-to-Q delay, minimum data-path delay, and fast-path on-chip variation derating factors) and must satisfy:

$$
T_{\text{arr, min}} \ge t_{\text{hold}} + t_{\text{skew}} + t_{\text{uncertainty}}
$$

preventing newly launched data from corrupting the captured value during the capture flip-flop's hold interval. Setup and hold checks evaluate orthogonal operating corners in multi-corner multi-mode analysis: setup checks stress slow process silicon under reduced supply voltage and elevated temperature (where propagation delays peak), whereas hold checks stress fast silicon under elevated voltage and sub-zero temperature (where short paths race the clock). A candidate that passes timing under a single nominal corner can severely fail under this multi-corner envelope. These inequalities cover the paths and checks enabled by the model and constraints. A `set_false_path` directive excludes matching paths from the specified timing analysis; it does not establish that the physical paths meet timing or report a meaningful zero slack for them. An unjustified exception can therefore remove a real violation from the report, as in the SDC defect class of @sec-semantic-rtl-defects. The engine may be following its inputs correctly while the checking setup omits a required obligation.

The same question, what the engine's model contains, decides what every check class can support and what it cannot establish on its own (@tbl-check-scope).
