| **Check class** | **What results support under declared conditions** | **What results cannot establish by themselves** |
| - | - | - |
| Syntax and interface | Adherence to schemas, grammatical rules, and port widths. | Functional correctness, performance, power, or physical feasibility. |
| Functional simulation | Execution behavior on explicit software binaries under model semantics. | Timing closure, physical cell layout, thermal stability, and unexecuted paths. |
| Hardware emulation | Long-trace execution behavior at high effective cycle counts. | Final physical timing closure, detailed routing constraints, and power dissipation. |
| Low-power static | UPF power domain intent and structural isolation rules. | Dynamic IR-drop, power-switch settling delays, and active energy consumption. |
| Formal verification | Proofs/counterexamples for explicit properties over bounded/unbounded models. | Objectives outside the property set, or behavior under violated assumptions. |
| Architectural models | Microarchitectural cycle timing for declared workloads (gem5, ChampSim). | Physical layout limits or behaviors outside validated model regions. |
| Physical analysis | Implementation and physical results under specified models: synthesis (Yosys), place-and-route (OpenROAD), physical signoff (geometric design rule checking and layout versus schematic verification via Calibre), STA (Tempus), power integrity (RedHawk-SC), and separately bound thermal analysis. | Missing constraints, functional intent, or unmodeled manufacturing variation. |
| Silicon telemetry | Measured behavior of fabricated parts under test conditions. | Unmeasured workloads, operating lifetimes, or uncharacterized parts. |
: **Checks are decisive only for the properties they observe.** Costlier or downstream tools do not widen property coverage. {#tbl-check-scope tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Stronger Claims Require Stronger Checks"}
**The principle:** Verification rigor must match the consequences and reversibility of the architectural decision.

**The application:** High-consequence decisions require checks suited to each material claim. Formal proofs, signoff reports, and silicon measurements address different obligations; none substitutes for the others merely because it is more rigorous or costly. Uncalibrated surrogate scores cannot justify such commitments.
:::

Inner-loop candidate screening tolerates bounded surrogate error, while revising a shared bus protocol requires checks of the affected behavioral and interface obligations, and freezing pinouts for tapeout requires the relevant implementation signoff checks. Structuring verification plans across explicit consequence tiers prevents under-checking high-risk commitments while avoiding the expense of running full signoff flows on early exploratory drafts (@tbl-feedback-by-consequence).

| **Intended use of result** | **Consequence if wrong** | **Feedback plan should include** |
| - | - | - |
| Local candidate screening | Wasted simulation budget or deferred promising candidates. | Candidate identity, matched comparator, and known proxy error bounds. |
| Shared interface revision | Downstream hardware/software work inherits errors. | Regression suites, interface compatibility checks, and explicit assumptions. |
| High-consequence commitment | Multimillion-dollar respin or tapeout failure. | Signoff checks covering all material claims, decision-margin bounds, and independent verifiers. |
: **Feedback plans must follow consequence and reversibility.** Verification rigor matches the cost of error propagation. {#tbl-feedback-by-consequence tbl-colwidths="[26,34,40]"}

Consequence and reversibility help set the required rigor. A wrong screen can waste evaluation budget or discard a useful candidate; a wrong tapeout decision can incur a mask respin and a long delay. Stronger checks reduce particular risks but do not establish zero residual risk. Adding checkers helps only to the extent that they contribute relevant information, since shared assumptions can leave shared failures unobserved.

### Correlated Blind Spots and Diverse Checkers {#sec-correlated-blind-spots}

Different implementations do not establish independent failure behavior, as multiversion-programming research cautions [@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion]. LLM evaluators can also favor their own generations [@PanicksseryEtAl2024SelfPreference]. For architectural verification, the practical question is which specification assumptions, model simplifications, or learned components the producer and checker share (@fig-independent-checks). Those dependencies can leave the same defect unchallenged even when the checks have different names.

![**A second check provides value only when it challenges an otherwise untested assumption.** Sharing a model or specification between producer and critic produces correlated agreement rather than independent validation (left). A claim-specific check using an orthogonal measurement path mounts a bounded challenge, though unexamined shared assumptions must still be recorded (right) [@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion; @PanicksseryEtAl2024SelfPreference].](images/fig-independent-checks){#fig-independent-checks width="80%" fig-alt="Two-column flow diagram contrasting correlated agreement from shared assumptions against a bounded challenge from an orthogonal checking path."}

Mutation testing in @sec-semantic-rtl-defects assessed an individual suite's sensitivity to defects; here the question is whether checkers miss the same defects. Mutation testing measures whether checks distinguish deliberately altered programs from the reference [@DeMilloLiptonSayward1978Hints]. Applying that idea to several checkers lets the verification team examine their joint escapes. When a non-equivalent injected RTL defect escapes both an automated formal assertion suite and a dynamic testbench, the joint escape demonstrates a shared detection gap for that fault. The cause still needs diagnosis, as both checks may inherit a specification omission or each may miss the fault for a different reason. Trace the escape through the asserted property, formal assumptions, test stimulus, and checked outputs to decide which check needs revision, then rerun the mutant to test whether that gap has closed. Agentic benchmark audits provide an adjacent warning, demonstrating that insufficient tests and reward rules accepting empty responses can inflate apparent success [@ZhuEtAl2025AgenticBenchmarks]. For RTL verification, stimulus must exercise the behavior whose correctness is claimed, and the checker must observe its effects. Test vectors that execute without exercising internal state transitions (such as testing an arithmetic pipeline with operand streams that never trigger carry generation, overflow saturation, or AXI backpressure valid-ready stalls) create a false impression of high verification pass rates while leaving logic defects unexercised.

Security properties expose another shared blind spot. Spectre and Meltdown demonstrated leakage through transient execution and microarchitectural side channels that ordinary checks of architectural outputs need not detect [@KocherEtAl2019Spectre; @LippEtAl2018Meltdown]. Suites checking only those outputs can therefore agree while leaving the relevant information-flow property unexamined. The noninterference example in @sec-formal-bounds-sequential-equivalence explains why inspecting isolated executions is insufficient for that property. In a search loop, an objective based only on throughput or power, performance, and area can favor changes to speculation, sharing, or mitigations without charging their security consequences. The verification plan needs checks matched to the threat model, such as a noninterference proof under declared speculative semantics, cache-timing-channel analysis, or a structural check for domain isolation. Repeating a functional test adds no direct coverage of an observation that test does not make.

## Routing Evidence Across System Layers {#sec-routing-evidence-layers}

Qualified signals need to reach the part of the design process that can act on them. A formal counterexample may call for RTL repair or specification revision; negative timing slack calls for timing diagnosis before choosing a repair; and an unresolved empirical delta may call for expanded trace sampling. Before routing a counterexample to specification revision, establish whether the specification misstates the intended contract or the RTL violates it. These actions change different objects, so combining every return into a scalar optimizer score would lose information needed for the next step. A *distribution shift* changes the workloads, tool versions, or operating conditions that generated the data a surrogate or claim was qualified on.[^fn-proxy-shift-c07] A known change in those conditions, or deteriorating agreement with new reference measurements, calls for requalification of the affected surrogate (@tbl-feedback-destinations).

[^fn-proxy-shift-c07]: **Proxy Gaps and Shift**: In ML terminology, covariate shift changes the input distribution while preserving the conditional distribution of the target given the inputs. A change in that conditional relationship is a different shift. Which description fits a workload or process change depends on the model's inputs and prediction target; the node name alone does not decide it.

| **Qualified or verified status** | **Implicated architectural object** | **Eligible next technical action** |
| - | - | - |
| **Proxy outside support** | Method choice or qualification study | Recalibrate, narrow, replace, or halt proxy use. Do not treat unsupported proxy outputs as training labels. |
| **Missing constraint** | Study formulation or representation | Record rationale and add missing constraint to representation. |
| **Resolved outcome, open mechanism** | Study formulation | Preserve result and add a distinguishing contrast before attributing the outcome to a mechanism. |
| **Unresolved comparison** | Measurement plan | Use further investigation allowed by the declared plan, or define a new comparison with its own budget and stopping rule. |
| **Difference below decision margin** | Study findings | Retain result without forcing architectural or model updates. |
| **Accepted bounded exception** | Design requirements and responsible owner | Record waiver scope, rationale, compensating control, and reopening trigger. |
: **Established status determines next technical actions.** Execution failures route to environment repairs; qualified results direct changes to the representation, study, or retained findings. {#tbl-feedback-destinations tbl-colwidths="[25,35,40]"}

Disagreement between checkers needs diagnosis before it drives a design change. Suppose a formal run reports Proved while simulation shows a miscompare. The methodology must first establish whether the proof covers the failing behavior under the simulation's inputs and conditions. Likewise, two proxies can rank a pair of candidates differently without either ranking identifying the cause of the disagreement. Their scope, reference agreement, and uncertainty need examination using @tbl-proxy-diagnostics. Retain both returns and their qualified limits while investigating the conflict. Until that conflict is explained, do not treat the disputed behavior or ranking as resolved or use it as a training label. Independently qualified reference measurements remain usable within their established scope.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Drive Actions Only from Qualified Results"}
**The principle:** Raw simulation logs and unparsed tool reports must never directly trigger design modifications or dataset updates.

**The application:** Only qualified statuses justify repairs, revisions, no-change decisions, or technical stops.
:::

Siemens Calibre Auto-Waivers provides a concrete example of retaining and applying geometric design-rule waivers [@SiemensCalibreAutoWaivers]. In the discipline proposed here, each accepted exception also retains its technical rationale, affected rule and design scope, any compensating controls, responsible owner, and reopening trigger. Spatial coordinates or identifying geometry belong in that scope where relevant. A waiver records a bounded exception; it does not turn the underlying violation into an unconditional pass.

## Propagating Feedback into Optimizer State {#sec-propagating-feedback-optimizer}

Routing qualified evidence determines what to retain about the design. It can also change how the search proposes its next candidate. These are related but distinct uses of feedback; a checked timing failure belongs in the study's findings, while the optimizer may use it to update a surrogate or choose another design. Unverified returns, transient execution errors, and biased candidate distributions can mislead those updates [@SculleyEtAl2015Hidden; @Settles2009ActiveLearning].

First distinguish adaptation within a declared method from replacing that method. Updating a Bayesian optimizer's posterior after a qualified measurement is part of its normal operation; it does not require a separate model-promotion exercise after every observation. The update rule, admitted measurements, and resulting state must remain inspectable. Changing the surrogate family, generator prompt, or search policy can instead alter the method being evaluated and may require a separate comparison before the revised version guides further work.

One implementation keeps proposed replacement versions in a shadow model registry, separate from the active search. Each version retains its data, settings, and intended use. A comparison against the active version then asks whether the change improves the relevant outcome: prediction error and screening decisions for a surrogate, or candidate quality and total evaluation cost for a generator or policy. A version that does not improve the declared criterion can remain inactive. This is a way to test a proposed change, not a universal requirement for every search-state update. The distinction between retaining findings and updating the search is summarized in @tbl-retention-vs-quarantine.

| **Dimension** | **Retained design findings** | **Search state and proposed method changes** |
| - | - | - |
| **Storage** | Existing experiment records, verification reports, and decision history. | Versioned search state; a separate registry for proposed replacement models or policies where useful. |
| **Contents** | Passed, failed, and inconclusive checks with their scope, assumptions, and candidate identities. | Surrogate weights, generator prompts, search trajectories, and the measurements admitted to each update. |
| **Integrity and qualification** | Version identities preserve traceability; technical checks establish what the findings support. | Declared update rules govern within-run adaptation; comparisons assess proposed method replacements. |
| **Reopening trigger** | Changed process corner, tool behavior, or ISA assumptions; license availability separately affects whether a rerun can execute. | Changed input conditions, or drift in residuals or empirical interval coverage measured against reference results. |
: **Design findings and search updates have different jobs.** Retained evidence records what was checked, while versioned search state makes the use of that feedback inspectable. A proposed method change still needs evaluation suited to its intended use. {#tbl-retention-vs-quarantine tbl-colwidths="[20,40,40]"}

Neither a separate registry nor an integrity hash establishes technical validity. An unsupported surrogate score cannot become a verified training label merely because it was stored separately. Similarly, a timing waiver needs a technical rationale and an authorized scope; its file hash only identifies the artifact. Evaluation cases kept out of training can still influence a method through repeated promotion decisions. Limit that adaptive reuse, refresh the confirmation cases, or use an inference procedure designed for it rather than assuming a nominal holdout remains independent indefinitely [@DworkEtAl2015ReusableHoldout].

Changes in workloads, tool versions, or PVT corners can invalidate the qualification on which dependent architectural claims rest [@QuinoneroCandelaEtAl2009DatasetShift]. Conformal prediction makes the need for reference measurements particularly clear. A conformal interval's coverage guarantee rests on exchangeability, the assumption that permuting the calibration points and the point being predicted does not change their joint distribution.[^fn-stats-conformal-prerequisites-c07] In active architectural search, two distinct mechanisms break this property. Exogenously, a change in workload regime (such as querying a latency surrogate calibrated on compute-bound SPEC CPU traces against irregular graph-analytics kernels with heavy cache-miss streams) introduces covariate shift. Endogenously, the search policy violates exchangeability when greedy candidate selection targets extreme predicted performance, systematically sampling points with extreme positive residual errors (the optimizer's curse). Under either mechanism, empirical coverage (the fraction of true values landing inside nominal $1-\alpha$ prediction bands) collapses without any internal warning from the surrogate itself [@TibshiraniEtAl2019CovariateShift]. The constructed coverage figure in @sec-support-limits illustrates this failure when the workload regime leaves the calibrated range.

Rolling empirical coverage measured against reference results can reveal the loss of coverage. That monitoring observes only the cases for which new reference results are collected, so a known change in operating conditions is itself reason to revisit qualification rather than wait for an alarm. The surrogate goes back through the proxy diagnostics of @tbl-proxy-diagnostics, matched reference measurements are taken at the new stratum, and its scores are trusted again only within the region those measurements cover. Widening a reported interval alone does not restore its coverage guarantee. Tracing claims to exact execution bindings limits the rerun work to the checks affected by the change.

[^fn-stats-conformal-prerequisites-c07]: **Conformal prediction prerequisites**: The standard finite-sample marginal coverage guarantee assumes exchangeability of calibration and test examples, meaning their joint distribution is invariant under permutation. Active optimization policies break exchangeability endogenously by conditioning subsequent queries on previous extrema, while workload and corner variations break it exogenously. Restoring valid coverage under these conditions requires weighted or adaptive conformal prediction [@TibshiraniEtAl2019CovariateShift]; widening static intervals does not recover the theoretical guarantee.

What a qualified result should change differs by scope. Within the run, it informs the next proposal. A realizable counterexample must be lifted into a generalized architectural constraint or inductive invariant before entering the represented state; injecting raw simulation traces or cycle-by-cycle error vectors directly into the generator prompt overfits to the specific trace without preventing structurally equivalent violations. A proxy found outside its support narrows the region the optimizer may trust; an unresolved delta may justify more samples rather than a design change. Across the project, the result changes the record. A Proved status discharges a scoped requirement, a waiver enters with its reopening trigger, and a result below the decision margin is retained without forcing an update. For later work, the useful material extends beyond surrogate weights or a winning configuration. The check that caught a defect, the mutant set that exposed a vacuous testbench, and the conditions under which a proxy was calibrated can guide a new study, subject to qualification in that setting.

Which of those retained items still holds when the workload, tool chain, or process node changes is the question distribution shift poses across problems rather than within one, and @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack takes it up under that name.

## Open Questions {#sec-feedback-open-questions}

Qualification exposes limits that remain difficult to bound as search changes the candidates, interfaces, and conditions being checked.

- **How can a timing surrogate bound false acceptance near zero slack?** A symmetric error measure assigns equal loss to 50\ ps of optimism and 50\ ps of pessimism, although the first can admit a timing violation and the second can reject a feasible candidate. Qualification on a fixed sample does not settle the risk when search repeatedly selects candidates near the optimistic edge. The unresolved problem is whether one-sided error bounds remain useful under that selection, and what reference measurements are needed to detect when their assumptions fail. This concerns the safety of the screening decision; the surrogate does not acquire the scope of a signoff timer.

- **How can a verification plan bound the blind spots its checks share?** Joint mutation testing exposes faults that escape both a simulation testbench and a formal assertion suite. Yet the mutants may encode the same interpretation of an ambiguous specification as both checkers, leaving an omitted requirement untouched. Independently developed contracts and challenges to specification assumptions could expose different gaps. The open issue is what coverage those methods can justify beyond the tested faults, especially when a generator introduces an interface the original verification plan did not anticipate.

- **How can early feedback qualify a new power-gating organization?** Static UPF checks can qualify declared power intent and structural isolation while leaving transient voltage droop and ground bounce during simultaneous domain wakeup unresolved. The chapter assigns those effects to physical analysis, but a search loop must choose which organizations to advance before every candidate receives detailed analysis. The research question is how conservative early models can identify unsafe wakeup behavior at useful cost, and which changes to domain structure or activity require renewed physical evaluation. A useful answer must state where the early model remains undecided.

- **When can a failed interface contract support a local repair?** Assume-guarantee reasoning separates a block's obligations from its assumptions about neighboring blocks. A failed assertion can nevertheless leave open whether to repair an internal transition, change the driving logic, or revise an inadequate contract. Diagnostic traces and targeted changes can distinguish some of these explanations, but may also reveal interacting causes. The unresolved issue is when that evidence is sufficient for local automated repair and when the system must investigate a coordinated interface redesign.

- **When is another checker worth its evaluation cost?** A checker can detect faults missed by the current suite, but its errors may also overlap with existing checks or reject useful candidates. Joint fault-detection measurements can characterize that contribution on known cases; they do not establish its value as the candidate distribution changes. The open problem is how to estimate the additional decision-relevant information well enough to allocate evaluation effort, while accounting for both missed defects and false rejections. Counting votes alone does not resolve that choice.

## Summary {#sec-trust-boundary-conclusion}

A tool return becomes evidence when its identity, conditions, status, and observational scope support the claim being made. For a formal result, qualification binds the property to its model, assumptions, and proof status. For a comparative measurement, it also requires a matched comparator, quantified uncertainty, and a declared decision margin. Keeping those requirements distinct lets an architect preserve a valid proof even when a performance comparison remains unresolved, or retain a measured gain without claiming unbounded correctness.

The qualified status determines the eligible next action. A counterexample can justify a repair or a revised architectural proposal, an unresolved comparison can justify more measurements, and a discrepancy between checkers calls for diagnosis before either result changes the design. Learning then operates at three scopes: the next proposal or check within the run, the findings retained across the project, and the checks or qualification conditions that may inform later work. Within-run updates follow the declared method, while proposed replacement models or policies need evaluation before their intended use. In either case, unsupported surrogate scores must not be treated as verified training labels. Each retained finding carries the conditions under which it can be reused.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Diverse checkers and mutation testing.** Use claim-specific verification paths and seeded faults to test whether agreement reflects fault detection. A passing mutant suite qualifies detection of the tested faults; shared omissions can remain.
- **Qualified evidence routing over raw returns.** Admit measurements under the criteria of @tbl-measurement-record and formal returns under their property, model, assumptions, and status. Route each according to the scoped claim it supports.
- **Proof and measurement answer different questions.** A completed unbounded proof establishes that an invariant holds across all reachable states within its declared assumptions. A comparative trade-off needs matched conditions, qualified workload and model scope, and a decision margin declared before measurement. Sampling or run variation also requires appropriate uncertainty characterization, such as a confidence interval; an exact deterministic score does not require a sampling interval.
- **Distinguish learning from evidence retention.** Preserve checked findings with their conditions, and record how they update the search. Separate ordinary adaptation under the declared method from proposed model or policy replacements, whose benefit still needs evaluation.
- **Strict separation of infrastructure error from design failure.** License preemption, cluster timeouts, and environment crashes route to environment repair rather than recording false hardware limit violations.
:::

With returns qualified, routed, and retained, @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack examines how these verification boundaries, execution harnesses, and learning mechanisms compose across the hardware-software stack.
